Ceres. A dwarf planet in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, and the largest body in that region. With a diameter of roughly 950 kilometers and a mass comprising roughly one-third of the asteroid belt's total mass, it was classified as an asteroid after its discovery in 1801, then reclassified as a planet briefly in the nineteenth century, and finally as a dwarf planet in 2006. The Dawn space probe revealed it to be geologically complex, with cryovolcanism, subsurface water ice, and bright mineral deposits.

Ceres was discovered on January 1st, 1801 by Giuseppe Piazzi. The naming follows the Roman goddess of agriculture, fitting for the first asteroid discovered. It is the most massive asteroid, constituting roughly 38 percent of the asteroid belt's total mass, far exceeding Vesta or any other belt resident. This dominance enabled its classification as a dwarf planet.

The asteroid is water-rich in composition. The surface and interior contain substantial water ice and hydrated minerals. Spectroscopy indicates clay minerals and carbonates, suggesting aqueous alteration. The Occator crater contains unusually bright deposits of salt-mineral residue, sodium carbonate, thought to be brine evaporite left by cryovolcanic activity.

Evidence suggests water-ice-rich magma erupted in the recent past. Ahuna Mons, a dome-shaped cryovolcanic feature, is geologically young, roughly 200 million years old. Ceres may be the remnant core of a proto-planet that never fully assembled due to Jupiter's gravitational perturbations.

Ceres is the gravitational center and mass anchor of the asteroid belt. It shares reclassification history with Pluto — both were demoted in 2006 under the same IAU rule. In the belt, Ceres stands in stark contrast to its nearest massive rival, Vesta, which is drier and more geologically rigid. The bright spots in the Occator crater are among the solar system's most reflective features.
